theme: Signs of Jerusalem’s siege; judgment is certain
readingInstruction: Read Ezekiel 4:1-7:27. God commands Ezekiel to act out the siege of Jerusalem in strange and difficult ways. Read these chapters as sermons without words, and then listen to the words in chapters 6 and 7, which say that the end has come.
settingTheScene: Ezekiel’s early prophecies, from 593 to 586 BC, are warnings of the fall of Jerusalem. The exiles in Babylon hoped that the city would be spared. Ezekiel’s task was to break that false hope. The sign-acts in chapter 4 and 5 are acted out for the exiles. He is bound, silent, and lying on his side, while they watch. The message is that the siege is coming and God himself is the enemy.
observation: “Take a brick and lay it before you and engrave on it a city, even Jerusalem” (4:1).
“Then lie on your left side… and I will lay the punishment of the house of Israel upon you” (4:4).
“And behold, I will put cords upon you, so that you cannot turn from one side to the other” (4:8).
“This is Jerusalem. I have set her in the center of the nations, with countries all around her” (5:5).
“Behold, I, even I, am against you” (5:8).
“And they shall know that I am the LORD” (6:7, a repeated refrain).
“An end! The end has come upon the four corners of the land” (7:2).
“Their silver and gold cannot deliver them in the day of the wrath of the LORD” (7:19).
interpretation:
Ezekiel’s sign-acts are strange. He draws Jerusalem on a clay brick and sets up a model siege around it. He lies on his left side for 390 days to bear the iniquity of Israel, and on his right side for 40 days for Judah. He eats rationed food baked over dung, a symbol of the defilement of exile. He shaves his head and beard with a sword and divides the hair into thirds: burned, struck with the sword, and scattered to the wind. The meaning is clear. Jerusalem will be besieged, starved, and destroyed. Only a few will survive.

The reason is in 5:5-8. Jerusalem was set in the center of the nations, to be a light. Instead, she has been more rebellious than the nations around her. “Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I, even I, am against you.” This is the stark reality: the one who had fought for Jerusalem is now fighting against her.

Chapter 6 addresses the mountains, because the people worshiped on the high places. It is an oracle to the land itself: the idols will be broken and the bones scattered. The refrain begins to appear: “Then you will know that I am the LORD.” This phrase occurs about sixty-five times in Ezekiel. The purpose of everything is the knowledge of God. Judgment and later salvation both serve this end.

Chapter 7 announces the end: “An end! The end has come.” The language is of a flood approaching. No one will go to battle, because God’s wrath is on all the multitude. Money and gold will be worthless. Famine and plague will fill the city. Even the temple will be profaned.

Why does Ezekiel tell us all this? Because the exiles needed to know that God does not lose control. The destruction of the temple was not a defeat for God. It was an act of God, the same God who loves them, and who will, in later chapters, restore.
connection: Jesus predicted the siege of Jerusalem in Luke 19:43-44 and Luke 21:20-24. In Mark 13, he warns that not one stone will be left. Hebrews 12:25-29 says our God is a consuming fire. John 8:28 shows that people will know who he is when the Son of Man is lifted up. Romans 11:22: “Note then the kindness and the severity of God.” Revelation 6:15-17 describes people hiding from the wrath of the Lamb.
application:
Reflect on the gravity of sin. Take time to confess something you might be treating lightly.

Ask what God might be teaching you through the “acts” of your own life, such as your family, work, and church.

Remember that every judgment in Ezekiel serves the purpose that people will know the LORD.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to keep you from treating his word lightly.
Ask him to teach you to fear him.
Tell him you know judgment is real.
